extracted.intended_audience: general readers seeking biographical and career information about Julia Sebutinde (students, journalists, researchers interested in international law)
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia biography of Julia Sebutinde covering her education, judicial career (including Special Court for Sierra Leone and the International Court of Justice), elections/appointments, controversies, and personal life.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICJ judges election requirement (absolute majority)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful candidate needs an absolute majority of votes both in the United Nations General Assembly and in the United Nations Security Council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page describes the 2011 election process as an example: candidates must obtain absolute majorities in both bodies concurrently; balloting can require multiple rounds (example: Sebutinde eventually received 97 of 193 votes in the General Assembly — the number required — and an absolute majority in the Security Council on resumed balloting). The election may leave vacancies if the required majorities are not achieved on a given day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination by national groups in the Permanent Court of Arbitration
rubrics_metrics.description: Candidates for the ICJ are nominated by national groups in the Permanent Court of Arbitration (the page notes Sebutinde was nominated by the national groups of Croatia, Denmark, and Uganda).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nomination by national groups is part of the ICJ candidate selection process prior to voting in the General Assembly and Security Council; the page uses Sebutinde's nominations as the factual instance of this procedural rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting presidency / line of succession at the ICJ
rubrics_metrics.description: When the ICJ President resigns, an acting president serves in accordance with the Court's acting line of succession until a new president is elected (page: 'she became the acting president upon president Nawaf Salam's resignation in accordance with the acting line of succession until Yuji Iwasawa's election').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article records the sequence: resignation by the sitting president, application of the Court's acting succession rules, and election of a new president to replace the acting incumbent. This illustrates the Court's internal procedure for continuity of leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial integrity: confidentiality, impartiality, and sub-judice conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial integrity demands strict confidentiality and impartiality; judges should not discuss matters that are sub-judice or comment on pending proceedings outside the Court (page quotes Sebutinde's statement asserting she 'did not, and would never, discuss outside of the Court any matter that is sub-judice').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page presents this as a normative standard for judges and as part of Sebutinde's rebuttal to media reports. It is invoked to counter allegations of bias or improper public comment and to emphasize expectations of judicial behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms for addressing alleged judicial partiality (remedial action requests)
rubrics_metrics.description: External bodies (e.g., International Commission of Jurists) can request remedial actions or removal of a judge from participation in specific proceedings on grounds of partiality, invoking relevant principles (the page references a communication urging removal and referring to Principles 17–20 of the UN Basic Principles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites the International Commission of Jurists' communication urging that the Court undertake remedial actions consistent with cited UN principles and requesting temporary removal of the judge from a particular case. This illustrates an accountability/remedy pathway used by external organizations when alleging bias.
